claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in tungsten-based plasma-facing structural materials are governed by dislocation climb mediated by enhanced vacancy diffusion at grain boundaries.
Dislocation climb allows dislocations to bypass second-phase dispersions or carbides.
Obstacle bypass by dislocation climb reduces flow stress.
Dislocation climb promotes dynamic recovery and thereby improves toughness.
Vacancy diffusion generally becomes significant in tungsten alloys above approximately 1000 °C.
Enhanced vacancy diffusion at grain boundaries facilitates dislocation climb.
Climb provides an alternative plasticity mechanism that bypasses obstacles.
Increased vacancy mobility at high temperature enables dislocations to climb around precipitates and intergranular barriers.
Climb around obstacles lowers the effective yield stress and increases plastic strain.
Dynamic recovery associated with dislocation climb delays crack initiation and propagation.
Relative to testing below approximately 800 °C, testing above approximately 1000 °C will produce lower flow stress.
Relative to the lower-temperature baseline, high-temperature testing will produce greater ductility and toughness.
High-temperature specimens will show dislocation debris and reduced dislocation pile-ups near obstacles as evidence of climb.
Below approximately 800 °C, vacancy diffusion and dislocation climb are not activated in the tungsten-based alloy.
Below approximately 800 °C, plastic strain in the tungsten-based alloy is primarily governed by dislocation glide.
The proposed mechanism applies when diffusion is sufficiently rapid and the material has a fine-grained microstructure containing dispersed obstacles.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to coarse-grained materials or when oxidation or other degradation mechanisms dominate.
Irradiation in a fusion environment could modify the proposed mechanism.
